summary: Looking for a Star is a high-performance interactive web tool developed for the direct visualization and analysis of raw astronomical data from NASA's SPHEREx mission, eliminating the reliance on local scientific computing environments. To address the computational complexity associated with this volume of spatial big data, the solution implements a hybrid architecture anchored by a FastAPI and Python backend with memory-optimized FITS matrix ingestion via astropy and numpy (memmap) and automated failover to a local cluster, coupled with a React and HTML5 Canvas frontend capable of rendering temporal sequences ("Flipbook") at over 10 FPS. Furthermore, it incorporates matrix processing for differential image subtraction, real-time generation of 102-band infrared spectral profiles, astrometric cross-validation against the ESA Gaia space catalog API, URL state synchronization, and automated audiovisual compilation via ffmpeg. The significance of this platform lies in its capacity to drastically lower computational entry barriers, enabling the distributed detection of celestial anomalies, near-Earth asteroids, and Planet X candidates within a rigorous citizen science framework.
details:
LOOKING FOR A STAR consists of a lightweight, interactive, public web tool designed to visualize massive datasets (FITS matrices) from NASA's SPHEREx mission directly in the browser, without requiring complex local installations or terminal commands. It operates through a "Flipbook"-style player that renders temporal sky sequences at over 10 FPS, enabling users to input coordinates (right ascension and declination) to travel through time, detect spatial anomalies, generate 102-band infrared spectra instantaneously, and validate findings against external catalogs. The benefits we offer are:

·       Scientific Democratization: Eliminates the steep technical barrier to entry so that any citizen or amateur astronomer can process spatial big data.

·       Efficiency and Speed: Allows seamless exploration of gigabytes of spatial information through in-memory optimization.

·       Automated Validation: Cross-references discovered data with external astronomical catalogs to confirm whether targets are known stars or genuine anomalies.

·       Outreach and Collaboration: Facilitates sharing discoveries through URL state synchronization and exporting timelines in MP4 video format for social media.

It is anticipated that the platform will mobilize and empower the global citizen science community (following the model of initiatives such as Backyard Worlds), enabling hundreds of thousands of volunteers to collaborate at scale with professional astronomers to discover comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs, and potential "Planet X" candidates hidden within the terabytes of data generated by the SPHEREx mission.

Technology Stack & Development Tools

Python was used as the primary programming language for the development of the project. The backend was built using FastAPI to handle rapid queries with an automatic failover system to a local cluster, integrating cutting-edge scientific libraries such as astropy and numpy for the in-memory processing of heavy FITS matrices using memmap=True, thereby preventing server overload. Meanwhile, the frontend was developed with React and HTML5 Canvas to ensure high-performance rendering of matrices converted into lightweight strings. Additionally, key external tools and APIs were integrated, including the ffmpeg engine to compile time sequences into downloadable MP4 videos and the European Space Agency's (ESA) Gaia space telescope API to perform astrometric validation of findings.

In What Sense Is Our Project Creative?

It stands out for its innovation in user experience and data processing through advanced features such as:

·       Mathematical Image Subtraction: Instead of displaying static images side by side, it subtracts spatial matrices in real time (Image B - Image A) to cancel out fixed stars (leaving a black background) and make the movement of an object or "Planet X" stand out instantaneously.

·       Real-Time Spectral Interactivity: Sums the data from all 6 infrared detectors upon clicking an object to display immediate spectral graphs.

·       Web Visual Optimization: Translates heavy scientific astronomical data into fluid visual dynamics accessible from a standard web browser.

 

What Factors Did Our Team Take into Account?

·       The Spatial Big Data Challenge: The need to efficiently manage and process massive volumes of data corresponding to more than one billion objects mapped every six months.

·       Accessibility for the Everyday User: Eliminating the need for advanced knowledge of command-line tools or massive multi-gigabyte downloads.

·       Scalability and Performance: Designing a hybrid backend and an optimized frontend capable of supporting rapid data updates and preventing NASA server saturation through an intelligent fallback system.

Potential Future Implementations (Evolution Roadmap)

·       AI Integration for Automated Discovery: Incorporate lightweight Machine Learning models in the browser or backend to automatically suggest moving anomalies or potential trans-Neptunian object candidates (such as Planet X), alerting the user in real time when mathematical subtraction detects unusual patterns.

·       Multi-Mission Compatibility and Expanded Cross-Catalogs: Expand the platform to cross-reference SPHEREx data not only with the Gaia telescope, but also dynamically integrate it with historical archives from missions such as WISE, Hubble, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), enabling deep multispectral analysis with a single click.

·       Collaborative and Social Mode (Citizen Science Hub): Develop a system of user accounts, profiles, and spatial bookmarks where citizens can report "candidate findings," tag discoveries, share annotated URL strings, and participate in community validation forums before escalating reports to professional astronomers.

·       Mobile Web Optimization and PWA (Progressive Web App): Evolve the frontend into a Progressive Web App that allows users to explore sky sequences and interact with the "Flipbook" player directly from mobile devices and tablets with full touch fluidity.

·       Batch Processing Assistant (Batch Export): Allow advanced users or educational institutions to schedule automated tasks to download or process entire regions of the sky in the background, facilitating its use in university classrooms and science outreach workshops.
